title: War machines can run amok with AI in control
teaser: New report reveals that much of modern military targeting is fully automated, leaving little room for human intervention—raising major concerns about AI's inherent flaws.
summary:
A new report by Airwars warns of the pervasive use of AI in modern warfare, demonstrating how machine learning now mediates nearly every step of a kill chain—from intelligence gathering to striking targets. The investigation found that many critical decisions are fully automated, limiting human intervention and raising concerns about 'automation bias.' Experts warn that this reliance on AI introduces inherent flaws, such as potential misidentifications from computer vision or inaccurate risk scoring based on social media data.

The authors stress looking at the entire stack of interconnected systems rather than single technologies. They argue that understanding these algorithms is crucial for public scrutiny regarding privacy and physical safety risks posed by automated warfare.
content: AIs not only make life-and-death targeting decisions on the battlefield, but also involve humans in only some stages of the decision-making process. To illustrate how that happens and prompt greater scrutiny of model-enabled killing, Airwars, a not-for-profit transparency watchdog, has published a detailed report, taking apart the ways machine learning powers modern warfare. The investigation, titled Anatomy of an AI Kill Chain , offers a visual guide through a fictitious kill chain - the steps real militaries go through to identify targets and eliminate them, with an emphasis on decisions delegated to AI. Authors Sophia Goodfriend, Heidy Khlaaf, Namir Shabibi, Joe Dyke, and Nathan Walker cover six stages: the decision support systems used to assist data gathering, surveillance technology, intelligence and identification, target selection, strikes on targets, and post-strike assessments. The report notes, "A recent book about US military AI revealed that in some operations only two of the six stages of the US military kill chain now involved humans in the loop, with a third involving some human oversight. The rest are now fully automated." Given that targeting mistakes have been widely documented , it's worth wondering whether AI is making such errors more common. And since military officials have, in the past, insisted AI's role cannot be known , there's reason to look for ways to better understand when AI is involved in life-and-death decisions. "In journalism and in policy, there's a tendency to focus on maybe one autonomous weapon system, like an Anduril drone or a Palantir anomaly detection system, and to look at the specific companies that are producing a few single machine learning algorithms that are undergirding those systems," said Sophia Goodfriend, research fellow at the University of Cambridge's Pembroke College and co-author of the report, in a phone interview with The Register . "What we wanted to do ... is to really underscore the stack of AI systems that are upending what it means to wage war, specifically what it means to surveil, target, and kill on the battlefield, and also emphasize how various technologies work together or don't work together throughout the kill chain." The project's goal, she said, is to look beyond specific technical systems at the way warfare is mediated by machine learning algorithms and to highlight the specific limitations of those systems. For each stage of the kill chain, the report touches on sources of potential errors: the reliability and accuracy of decision support systems, automated translation errors during surveillance of a target's text messages, target risk scoring systems derived from algorithmic assessment of social media data, computer vision systems that may misidentify objects and people, the shortcomings of recurrent neural networks used during drone strikes when there's GPS and/or electronic jamming, and the potential problems with AI-assisted battle damage assessment systems. The specific kill chain described is fictitious, but Goodfriend said that this was necessary to avoid making overreaching claims about how specific militaries operate. "Obviously it's hard to reconstruct proprietary systems used by militaries in real time today because they are often censored and secret and reporters cannot pry open exactly how a military is operating," she said, adding that she hopes the report prompts people to question claims about having a human in the loop. "What comes across in this piece is just how difficult it is for a human to intervene in a machine learning decision, the pernicious problem of automation bias, especially under the time constraint of war, and just how thoroughly everything is mediated by AI and automation already on the battlefield," she said. "So even if you have somebody who's reviewing a risk profiling system by looking at a social media post, that social media post will be translated by a machine learning algorithm and they won't be able to verify if that translation is correct because they're dealing with this time constraint and it will be really tempting and much easier to defer to an AI-generated output." Goodfriend acknowledges that it's difficult for civilians to make decisions about technologies they use that might amplify physical safety risks from military AI systems. That's why, she said, it's important to draw attention to the way these systems work. "The stack of AI systems integrated into warfare are the subject of a lot of hype and a lot of mystique and it's rare for those making or deploying these systems to really break down how they actually operate it and what it entails for civilians living under warfare," she said. "So, in illustrating how these technologies work, the massive amounts of data, of people's private information, of passive surveillance that is the foundation and lifeblood of automated warfare, I think that that's one way of moving the needle in terms of advocacy." The other key takeaway of the report, she said, is to underscore that machine learning systems make errors. "The point is not that these are teething problems that will be mitigated or ironed out once these technologies are deployed more and refined more, but really to emphasize the inherent flaws of machine learning and how they can't perform the tasks that militaries expect them to perform when they're deployed on the battlefield," she said. ®

title: MCP startup Runlayer accuses Rippling of stealing its product idea
teaser: In a lawsuit over IP theft, Runlayer accuses Rippling of cloning its Model Context Protocol gateway in a battle for AI infrastructure dominance.
summary: Startup Runlayer is suing HR software company Rippling for allegedly misappropriating its intellectual property (IP) after an extensive product trial. Runlayer provides a Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway—a standard for letting AI models access secure external data and tools. The suit claims that shortly after the collaboration, Rippling began developing a product that was 'almost a 1 to 1 copy' of Runlayer’s offerings. Rippling has confirmed launching its own MCP gateway but denies the theft, asserting they are building a superior product with proprietary information. This high-stakes legal dispute highlights the competitive and challenging nature of selling complex AI infrastructure into enterprise clients, a sector where adoption is slow even after deep technical trials.
author: Julie Bort
content: Runlayer, a startup that offers a secure Model Context Protocol gateway - a standard for letting AI models and agents securely pull in outside data and tools - has filed a lawsuit against HR software startup Rippling, according to the complaint seen by TechCrunch. The lawsuit is a cautionary tale for anyone selling AI infrastructure to enterprise customers, especially to other tech companies, that increasingly have the engineering muscle to just build the thing themselves. In the suit, Runlayer describes an extensive product trial conducted by Rippling as a prospective customer, during which the MCP startup shared everything from its product roadmap to its actual source code. The parties signed a mutual non-disclosure agreement and Rippling signed a product trial agreement with a clause that forbade it from copying Runlayer's intellectual property or making derivative works, which is standard boilerplate in enterprise software trials. Runlayer says in the complaint that Rippling's evaluation involved "nearly a year of intensive engineering collaboration." But in the end, the two could not agree on a price, so Runlayer ended the product trial. Shortly after that, Runlayer alleges that a "Rippling insider" texted Runlayer founder and CEO Andrew Berman to inform him of "a project internally to build essentially a clone o[f] Runlayer ... it's almost a 1 to 1 copy of Runlayer." Runlayer claims in the suit that Rippling's product must have been based on the startup's intellectual property and therefore constitutes trade secret misappropriation, unfair competition, and breach of contract. Rippling has confirmed to TechCrunch that it is indeed launching its own MCP gateway, though a spokesperson denies Runlayer's allegations about misusing its IP. "Runlayer's panicked effort to avoid competition by fabricating claims is not an effective way to deal with its business failures. Rippling is launching a superior product for connecting AI tools to business data using only our proprietary information - we have every reason to win in this market," a Rippling spokesperson tells TechCrunch. Runlayer has retained white-shoe law firm Sullivan & Cromwell. That doesn't mean Runlayer will, or even should, win this suit, but the same way a marquee VC lends a startup some credibility, a marquee law firm lends a lawsuit some credibility, at least optically. The more interesting part about this suit is really the inside peek it provides at the trials and tribulations of selling complex AI infrastructure into the enterprise, particularly to other tech companies. Enterprise sales notoriously take a long time to close, often because they hinge on this kind of deep, hands-on trial. MCP gateways in particular are getting crowded. Anthropic launched MCP as an open source protocol in November 2024. It's now one of the basic building blocks of AI interoperability, giving models and agents a secure way to access external data sources and services. MCP gateway products add control, security, and other features, especially for managing agents, and the field has grown considerably more competitive since Runlayer launched its product in the middle of last year and raised a total of $42 million , including from Khosla Ventures and Felicis. Even after an intense trial, an enterprise may simply opt to build the tool in-house. Both sides are stuck between a rock and a hard place.

title: The union drive at the Wikimedia Foundation is expanding
teaser: After UK staff started unionizing, US employees joined Wikimedia, but management refused recognition, leading to accusations of 'classic union-busting rhetoric' from workers.
summary: Unionization efforts have expanded at the Wikimedia Foundation, with US-based employees joining the drive following UK staff's initial organizing in June. However, management has refused voluntary recognition, leading organizers (affiliated with CWA) to accuse the nonprofit of using 'classic union-busting rhetoric.' The Foundation responded by stating that a secret ballot election via the NLRB is the proper path forward. These intense labor tensions highlight a broader conflict between the foundation and its thousands of unpaid volunteer contributors, escalating after hundreds of editors threatened strikes in May over the dissolution of an engineering team.
author: Mia Sato
content: In June, UK staff at the nonprofit that runs Wikipedia became the first to announce their intention to form a union . Now, US-based employees at the Wikimedia Foundation are joining the union drive, but management at the nonprofit has declined to voluntarily recognize their union. "While the Wikimedia Foundation touts to the public that they plan to take a neutral stance in our organizing efforts, they have already proven that not to be the case behind the scenes," a press release sent by Communications Workers of America, with which Wiki Workers United is affiliated, reads in part . "When the Foundation rejected our request for voluntary recognition this week, they immediately sent out to employees and the public statements couched in classic union-busting rhetoric, rhetoric undoubtedly provided by outrageously expensive union-avoidance law firms. This insulting and wasteful use of Foundation resources is both an insult to Foundation employees and to the Free Knowledge Movement as a whole." In a public statement, the foundation said it believes a secret ballot election with the NLRB is the "appropriate path forward." The unionization efforts come at a time when tensions are high between the foundation and the thousands of unpaid volunteers who edit, write, and maintain Wikipedia. In May, hundreds of Wikipedia editors threatened to go on strike after the foundation dissolved an engineering team that worked closely with volunteers. Some volunteers questioned whether the layoffs were related to union efforts, which the foundation denied.

title: Bot-detection startup Spur nabs $200M from Insight
teaser: Bot detection startup Spur raised $200M; tech helps fight threats after bots passed human activity online.
summary: Cybersecurity startup Spur Intelligence secured $200 million in funding, led by Insight Partners. Founded by former Defense Department engineers in 2017, Spur specializes in detecting sophisticated bot traffic to safeguard enterprises from fake users and threats. This technology is critically needed because the scale of malicious activity has rapidly grown. Notably, Cloudflare reported that as of mid-2026, bot traffic surpassed human activity on the internet for the first time in history.
author: Julie Bort
content: Spur Intelligence, a cybersecurity startup based in Lake Mary, Florida, has raised a $200 million round led by Insight Partners. Spur, founded by two former Defense Department engineers in 2017 - five years before ChatGPT's public launch - was prescient. The startup's tech helps enterprises distinguish legitimate human users from increasingly well-hidden bot traffic to help identify fake users and threats. "As sophisticated criminal VPNs, residential proxy networks, and anonymization infrastructure proliferate, organizations are increasingly operating with a critical blind spot: they can see the activity, but not the infrastructure behind it," Insight's Thomas Krane said in a written statement. Detecting malicious traffic has, of course, been a hill corporate security teams have been climbing for eons. But nothing compares to the onslaught facing them today. As of mid-2026, bots are now more active on the internet than humans, Cloudflare reported last month. "Thought it would be end of 2027, then early 2027, but agentic traffic growing so fast that bots have now passed human traffic online for the first time in the Internet's history," Cloudflare founder and CEO Matthew Prince posted on X last month , pointing to his company's latest traffic report.

title: PayPal tops Q2 estimates and raises full-year forecast amid Stripe takeover bid
teaser: Despite a $53B takeover bid, PayPal beat earnings estimates on strong Q2 numbers, boosting confidence in its strategic turnaround.
summary: Despite facing a high-stakes $53 billion takeover bid from Stripe and Advent, PayPal reported robust Q2 results, with adjusted earnings of $1.38 per share on $8.68 billion in revenue. Key growth areas included Buy Now Pay Later volume, which jumped 26%. CEO Enrique Lores announced increased full-year guidance, signaling confidence in the company's AI-focused turnaround plan, aiming for at least $1.5 billion in savings. The positive financial performance strengthens PayPal’s stance, as its board views the reported buyout offer as undervaluation and has historically held out for a significantly higher price.
author: Duncan Riley
content: Shares in PayPal Holdings Inc. closed regular trading up 4% today after the payments company beat expectations on revenue and earnings in its second quarter and raised its full-year profit forecast, less than two weeks after a $53 billion buyout offer from Stripe Inc. and Advent International L.P. that its board considers too low. For the quarter ended on June 30, PayPal reported adjusted earnings of $1.38 per share, down 1% from a year earlier, on revenue of $8.68 billion, up 5%. Analysts were expecting $1.28 per share on revenue of $8.47 billion. On an unadjusted basis, net income fell 12% to $1.1 billion, or $1.25 per share. Total payment volume rose 10% to $486.4 billion and payment transactions rose 8% to 6.8 billion. Active accounts were up 0.3% year-over-year at 439 million, though the figure slipped by about 200,000 from the first quarter. Profitability moved the other way. Adjusted operating income fell 8% to $1.5 billion. Adjusted operating margin contracted 248 basis points to 17.4%. Transaction margin dollars rose 1% to $3.9 billion. That is the number Chief Executive Enrique Lores has put at the center of his turnaround plan. Branded checkout volume grew 2% on a currency-neutral basis, the second quarter in a row it has managed that. The business has been the sore point in PayPal's core for years. Growth was faster elsewhere. Buy now, pay later volume jumped 26%. Venmo and Braintree both grew in the mid-teens. Lores, who replaced Alex Chriss in February, said PayPal had "moved with urgency" during the quarter to sharpen its transformation plan. Branded checkout, in his words, has "further stabilized." That plan targets at least $1.5 billion in cost savings over two to three years, with $400 million of it identified for 2026. Chief Financial Officer Jamie Miller told analysts on a conference call that the aim is faster transaction margin growth over time from a wider set of revenue streams. Guidance went up too. PayPal put full-year adjusted earnings at about $5.38 per share. Its earlier forecast had run anywhere from a low single-digit decline to slightly positive growth. The full-year transaction margin dollars target went to $15.6 billion. For the third quarter, the company guided to a low-single-digit percentage decline in adjusted earnings from $1.34 a year ago. PayPal bought back about 33 million shares during the quarter, spending $1.5 billion. It also declared a dividend of 14 cents per share, payable Sept. 25 to holders of record as of Sept. 4. The results land in the middle of a takeover fight. Stripe and Advent bid $60.50 per share for PayPal on July 15 and were reportedly turned down on July 20 , with the board holding out for a price closer to $70. Cantor Fitzgerald & Co. analyst Ramsey El-Assal put together a peer-multiple sum-of-the-parts valuation the day after the offer surfaced, covering Venmo, branded checkout and Braintree, that implied roughly $70 a share would more fully reflect PayPal's intrinsic value. His price target on the stock is $54 and his rating is neutral. title: Cyera to buy nonhuman identity startup Oasis Security for a reported $1B
teaser: With nonhuman identities exploding by nearly 500%, data security firm Cyera is acquiring Oasis Security to govern the powerful but risky rise of AI agents in enterprise systems.
summary: Data security company Cyera announced its acquisition of Oasis Security, a startup specializing in non-human identities. This move addresses the rapid proliferation of AI agents (bots, APIs) in corporate systems. Cyera’s CEO noted that nonhuman identities grew nearly 500% in six months, making governance critical. The deal is reported to be worth around $1 billion, combining Oasis's tools—which inventory and police credential usage—with Cyera's platform for sensitive data classification. This merger provides a single control point necessary to manage the risks posed by autonomous agents.
author: Duncan Riley
content: Data security company Cyera Ltd. revealed today that it is set to acquire nonhuman identity management startup Oasis Security Ltd. in a deal Israeli media report is worth about $1 billion. Neither company disclosed terms. Calcalist put the price at roughly $700 million in cash, with the rest paid in Cyera shares. Globes reported that the two have signed a letter of intent and that Oasis will run as an independent unit inside Cyera once the deal closes. Oasis Chief Executive Danny Brickman and Amit Zimerman started Oasis in 2022. Both are alumni of Israeli military intelligence Unit 81. The company sells tooling that inventories and polices the credentials machines use to sign in to corporate systems. Service accounts, application programming interfaces, bots and workloads all authenticate with no person behind them, and Oasis maps what each one is able to reach. Dormant accounts get flagged. So do over-broad permissions and badly configured credentials. The platform can rotate or retire those credentials without a human in the loop. That problem has grown considerably as enterprises hand work to autonomous agents. Cyera said nonhuman identities inside Fortune 500 companies grew nearly 500% over the past six months and are now the fastest-growing identity type in the enterprise. Buying Oasis bolts identity governance onto a platform built to find and classify sensitive data, giving Cyera a single control point for deciding what an agent is allowed to reach. "Knowing your data isn't enough if you can't govern who or what touches it," Cyera Chief Executive Yotam Segev wrote in a blog post announcing the deal. Identity data has the reverse problem, he added, telling a security team who is asking without telling it what they can see. Segev also warned that agents are arriving faster than teams can govern them and that an agent does not have to be attacked to do damage. Cyera itself dates to 2021, founded by Segev and Chief Technology Officer Tamar Bar-Ilan. Its platform crawls enterprise systems looking for sensitive information and judging how securely that information is held. Unencrypted records and weak access controls can be fixed automatically. A separate product, AI Guardian, checks whether AI agents are complying with enterprise data policy. The company has been buying steadily. Cyera acquired data security startup Trail Security Ltd. for $162 million in 2024 , data lake company Ryft Data Inc. in April and Genie Security in May , alongside earlier deals for Otterize Inc. and Shape AI Ltd . It has the balance sheet to keep going. Cyera raised $600 million in June at a $12 billion valuation in a round led by Evolution Equity Partners, taking its total raised to roughly $2.3 billion. Oasis had raised $190 million before the acquisition. Its most recent round, a $120 million Series B announced in March , was led by Craft Ventures Management with participation from Cyberstarts, Sequoia Capital Operations and Accel Partners LP. "From day one, we recognized that non-human identities would become one of the key security challenges of the AI era," Brickman said in comments reported by Calcalist. title: An Exclusive Preview of My Next Video
teaser: Creator announces simulating epidemics on the rebuilt Liberty City map using thousands of SEIR model simulations.
summary: Content creator Tivadar from The Palindrome announced a massive upcoming project: simulating epidemic dynamics using a reconstructed Liberty City map (from Grand Theft Auto). He ran thousands of simulations, applying the SEIR model to study how diseases spread and how control measures impact those spread patterns. To fund this ambitious content, which is supported exclusively by paid subscriptions, Tivadar offered an exclusive promotion: a 36% discount on all memberships until July 31st.
author: The Palindrome
content: Hey! It's Tivadar from The Palindrome. I've been working on my next video for quite a while. It's one of my biggest projects yet. This time, I rebuilt the Liberty City map from the first installment of Grand Theft Auto - and decided to run thousands of simulations to study the dynamics of epidemics and the effect of control measures. Even though the video is not yet ready, I want to give you an exclusive sneak peek! title: Logitech’s handheld plans are on ice — don’t expect a G Cloud 2 soon
teaser: Despite enthusiasm for handheld gaming, Logitech’s new boss confirms plans for a successor to the G Cloud are currently 'on ice.'
summary: During an interview, Logitech's new global head of Gaming, Robin Piispanen, stated that the company is postponing plans for a successor to its streaming handheld, the G Cloud. Although he finds the concept 'charming,' several hurdles—including high local hardware costs and incomplete cloud infrastructure from providers like Microsoft or Tencent—make development unfeasible right now. He pointed out that while cloud solutions solve physical limitations (weight, battery), they are hampered by cost and reliability. Piispanen confirmed Logitech's continued interest in partnering with major players on future cloud gaming platforms, seeing it as the most viable path forward for the company.
author: Sean Hollister
content: Logitech's new gaming boss, Robin Piispanen, tells me he likes the idea of gaming handhelds. "It's such a charming value proposition," he says, as we sip iced vanilla lattes at my local cafe. But he's not building one right now. He's not sure when or if Logitech should try again, after its underwhelming experiment with the Logitech G Cloud streaming handheld. "Right now, in this moment in time, there's bigger things for us to focus on than doing a second G Cloud," he tells me. Personally, I feel like the G Cloud would have a better chance today. At its 2022 debut , the $350 Logitech handheld was almost completely overshadowed by the far more capable $400 Steam Deck, whose PC chip could keep on playing games without needing reliable internet. But today, the price of a Steam Deck has risen to $789. The golden age of handhelds is over , and "the new normal" can be prohibitively pricey . Sony recently suggested that cloud gaming handhelds like its own PlayStation Portal are one possible hedge against RAMageddon. "Cloud streaming also requires minimal memory, making it an increasingly attractive low-cost thin client device in the current market environment where memory prices are rising," said a top PlayStation exec in a recent business meeting. Last year, I discovered Nvidia's GeForce Now had advanced far enough to breathe new life into existing handhelds . But it sounds like Logitech got burned by its first Tencent-backed attempt with the original G Cloud. Even people who bought it weren't necessarily satisfied. While there was a "realm of players that was super dedicated and loved it," says Piispanen, it didn't have staying power for the vast majority of buyers. "The bigger portion, call it the 80 percent, bought it, tried it, and then it ended up in a drawer." "We tried something that we really believed in, and it didn't really materialize into the use case people wanted," he says. The other problem was that the big cloud gaming providers didn't build out enough infrastructure quickly enough. "Cloud gaming in general really stagnated," he says, adding later: "Microsoft clearly said cloud is expensive, cloud gaming is expensive to run." Would Logitech consider building a standalone handheld instead, then, using the lessons it learned from the G Cloud? Piispanen's not sure about that. He says it's theoretically possible, something to perhaps look into. But he says Logitech's core competencies are design and input, and it'd probably partner with another company for the rest. Robin Piispanen is the new global head of Logitech G, taking over after long-time leader Ujesh Desai's retirement. Piispanen joined Logitech in 2008. Photo: Logitech He says handhelds don't look like a particularly good business to break into, anyhow: "The handheld only works when you get to a really big scale, and most of the handheld companies also own the content. So the question is then, should I get into content? Look at Nintendo, they own the content. Look at Steam." His question is just rhetorical, though. We quickly agree that buying studios hasn't worked out great for Sony and Microsoft recently, and he doesn't seem interested in competing with Asus and its Xbox Ally X . "They operate on slim margins and they don't own anything. They have to work with everyone else to make it work. It's not an easy business." If Logitech were to try handhelds again, he thinks that cloud gaming might still be the way forward - just not quite yet. "Cloud solves weight, it solves battery power, it solves graphics. It solves a lot of things... when you play locally, you don't have those barriers." He says, cryptically, that Logitech is investing in the future of cloud despite how the G Cloud turned out, and is actively talking to big players. "We talk to Microsoft, Tencent, and all of them: what do they see? How would this become a bigger play? And then see how we can potentially be a part of that." Does he see an inflection point where cloud infrastructure costs drop dramatically? Is there a point in the next few years where a whole bunch of Nvidia AI data centers are going to age out and become useful for gaming instead? He says he agrees with my "future casting," but can't say when it might happen. "If you figure it out, please let me know," Piispanen says. I spoke to Logitech's new gaming boss about other topics too; stay tuned to The Verge later today for more tidbits from our chat! title: You don’t need to splurge on an expensive handheld fan to beat the heat
teaser: Don't splurge on expensive handheld fans: Affordable alternatives beat Dyson in battery life and value for summer adventures.
summary: Consumers don't need expensive personal cooling devices like the $99.99 Dyson HushJet Mini Cool. The article reviews affordable alternatives, finding that the budget-friendly JisuLife Life10 S fans are highly effective for daily use. Although the Dyson fan is powerful, it is loud and its battery life is significantly shorter (e.g., over an hour at full power). In contrast, the JisuLife fan boasts impressive endurance, running for over 16 hours at half power. The author notes that while high-end options like the SharkChillPill are effective, the reliable and affordable JisuLife alternative provides adequate cooling without the major expense or noise associated with premium brands.
author: Andrew Liszewski
content: Despite what influencers may say, you don't need to spend $99.99 on Dyson's HushJet Mini Cool or $149.99 for the Shark ChillPill to survive the summer whenever you leave the comfort of air-conditioning. My family has found all the comfort it needs to survive humid baseball games, sweltering concerts, and sweaty hikes with a couple of affordable handheld fans from a Chinese company called JisuLife that has spent the past decade honing its hardware. At the start of the summer, I impulse-purchased a pair of JisuLife Life10 S fans from Costco, which at CDN $25 each (or $32.99 through Amazon ), are among the most basic offerings from the company. JisuLife's extensive lineup includes some fan models costing close to $100 with features like reverse-charging to power your phone and 100 different speed settings. I want all those features, but my goal was to not spend several hundred dollars on personal cooling devices that could easily go missing or get damaged during the chaos of summer activities. On the back of the fan is a USB-C charging port and a sliding power switch that prevents the fan from accidentally turning on while it's being jostled around inside a bag. The Life10 S' functionality is comparatively basic, but also easy to use. A sliding power switch on the back prevents it from accidentally turning on while banging around inside a backpack, and a single button on the front cycles through five different fan speeds. There's also a basic LCD display showing the battery's remaining charge when the fan is first powered on and the current speed setting. It's simple, but the Life10 S does its one job quietly and for a surprisingly long time. A single button cycles through the fan's five different speed settings. When Dyson announced its first handheld fan in April, I assumed the company that had developed an expertise in moving air had created a personal cooling device that would outperform everything else on the market. My spouse loves their Dyson hair dryer, and I was sure the HushJet Mini Cool would be my secret weapon for surviving hot and humid summers, even if at $99 it was a splurge. But having used both Dyson's personal fan and JisuLife's $25 alternative, I only reach for the latter when braving the world without AC. The basic LCD display on the front of the fan is sometimes hard to see because it's hidden behind a reflective black cover, but the fan is easy to use without being able to see it. Dyson's HushJet Mini Cool wraps impressive engineering in an eye-catching design, and at its highest setting, it easily out blasts JisuLife's even with the Life10 S set to full power. But even at its lowest setting, the HushJet is loud with a high-pitched whine reminiscent of Dyson's vacuums. I don't mind that sound when it's limited to short bursts of cleaning at ground level, but not when coming from a tiny fan designed to be used close to your face and ears. The JisuLife fan produces sound at a much lower frequency, making it easier to tolerate for hours, even if it's far from whisper quiet at full power. What impresses me more about the JisuLife fan is how long its 5,000mAh battery keeps it running. At half power, which we find is strong enough to cool us down on even the hottest days, the fan ran for just over 16 hours before needing a charge. That's far longer than my son lasted at the water park. For comparison, Dyson estimates the HushJet Mini Cool will run for up to six hours at its lowest setting, and at full power, I had it die after just over an hour. I haven't tested the even pricier Shark ChillPill that combines a fan with a metal cooling plate the company claims can lower skin temperature by up to 16 degrees Fahrenheit in seconds. You can cool down by pressing it all over your body, but it only cools for as long as the fan has power. SharkNinja estimates the ChillPill will run for up to 11 hours at its lowest setting, or just an hour-and-a-half at max power. That approach could be very effective, but I'm not spending $150 to find out. I've also tested the wearable neck fans that seem to be very popular among the cashiers at my local Costco, but I didn't find them to be as effective as I'd hoped. The breeze is spread out across the length of the fan and doesn't feel as intense as a handheld fan, and wearing it positions the motor right below your ear at all times, so it's a constant drone. I see why they're useful, but it's not an experience anyone in my family enjoyed. After a successful summer with these fans, I'm already keeping an eye out for sales on other JisuLife models, including a hands-free version you wear hanging from your neck . But I'm also expecting these cheaper alternatives will continue to be the first thing we pack when heading out on adventures for the rest of the summer and probably for years to come. title: Deep space dishes dodge devastation from Spanish wildfires
teaser: Critical space dishes, including those serving the European Space Agency and NASA, largely dodged devastation from Spanish wildfires.
summary: NASA’s Deep Space Communications Complex (MDSCC) and ESA's Cebreros antenna successfully navigated recent Spanish wildfires. While some cable damage was reported at the Madrid site, officials confirmed no significant structural damage to major antennas or buildings. The critical nature of this infrastructure meant that mission support seamlessly transitioned to other global facilities in Goldstone, California, and Canberra, Australia, ensuring continuous spacecraft communication for NASA's Deep Space Network (DSN). Furthermore, ESA declared Cebreros antenna 'GREEN' for nominal operations, maintaining service continuity for missions like Mars Express. The MDSCC features several large antennas, including DSS-63, which has a diameter of 70 meters.
content: SCIENCE Deep space dishes dodge devastation from Spanish wildfires NASA reports some cable damage near Madrid as its antennas and ESA's Cebreros station emerge largely intact Radio antennas for the European Space Agency and NASA appear to have escaped the worst effects of wildfires in Spain, though NASA's site sustained some cable damage. Over the weekend, a NASA spokesperson confirmed there was "no significant structural damage observed to antennas or buildings" at the Madrid Deep Space Communications Complex (MDSCC) despite fire ravaging the area. The spokesperson cautioned that "the situation remains dynamic" and additional inspections are required. A source with knowledge of the matter has since told The Register that the antennas had indeed escaped the worst of the inferno. They said, "All the stations are built to withstand every form of nature." The facility is part of NASA's Deep Space Network (DSN), which is used to communicate with spacecraft. According to the spokesperson, "NASA's Space Communications and Navigation (SCaN) Program has seamlessly transitioned mission support to its other Deep Space Communications Complexes in Goldstone, California, and Canberra, Australia, ensuring continuity of operations and uninterrupted spacecraft communications." Not counting the big dish at Goldstone, of course, on which more below. The European Space Agency (ESA) also has a facility in the area. Its Cebreros antenna, located approximately 77 km west of Madrid, was also at risk from the wildfires but was "declared GREEN for nominal operations" as of yesterday, according to ESA boss Josef Aschbacher. The Cebreros station , also known as Deep Space Antenna 2, marked 20 years since its inauguration in September 2025. It is used for communications with missions including Mars Express and Solar Orbiter. NASA's Madrid Deep Space Communications Complex has several antennas, including DSS-63, an antenna with a diameter of 70 meters. NASA has two other 70-meter antennas, at Goldstone in California and Canberra in Australia. All were originally built as 64-meter-diameter dishes, but were expanded to 70 meters from 1982 to 1988 to increase their sensitivity to support Voyager 2's encounter with Neptune. The 70-meter antenna at Goldstone was damaged last year after it over-rotated while supporting the Juno mission. There were no injuries, but NASA classed it as a "Type A mishap" and noted excessive stress on the structure and the facility's cables, as well as damage to the fire suppression system, which caused "significant flooding." Repairs and upgrades are expected to be completed by October 2028. ®

content: The first modern GPU with 4GB of VRAM has appeared, as RAM prices and component shortages push tech prices higher. content: Apple's latest AirTag may seem like the obvious choice if you own an iPhone and are shopping for a Bluetooth tracker, but it's not the most affordable option. It works well across both platforms, and right now it's on sale for $23.99 ($11 off) at Amazon and directly from Tile .
